video_title: Billionaire David Booth Lost To the Market for 9 Years. He Never Changed His Mind.
gist: David Booth, founder of Dimensional Fund Advisors (which crossed $1 trillion AUM in February 2026), recounts DFA's brutal first 9-year small-cap drought (2% vs. the S&P 500's 14% annualized return), the origins of indexing at Wells Fargo, and how the Fama-French three-factor model shaped DFA's value strategies. He argues for owning the whole market rather than picking AI winners, reframes investing success as judging decisions rather than outcomes, and stresses that real patience — often decades, not years — is the actual edge in factor investing.

themes.theme: Origins of Indexing at Wells Fargo & the Birth of Dimensional

insights.claim: David Booth started at Wells Fargo's trust department in September 1971, the same month the firm launched its first indexed portfolio (the Samsonite account), working alongside outside consultants Fisher Black and Myron Scholes while they simultaneously developed the Black-Scholes option pricing model.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Illustrates how tightly interwoven the origins of modern quantitative finance (indexing, options pricing) were within a single Wells Fargo working group in the early 1970s.
insights.quote: I started in September of '71, the same month that they started their first indexed portfolio for the Samsonite account.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 index fund built inside Wells Fargo's trust department by the same group Booth worked in was later sold off multiple times and eventually became the cornerstone of what is now BlackRock's indexing business.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Traces a direct lineage from a single early-1970s Wells Fargo project to the largest asset manager in the world today, useful context for understanding index-fund industry history and consolidation.
insights.quote: The S&P 500 index fund at the trust department was actually sold off a couple of times, ended up it's the cornerstone of BlackRock now.

insights.claim: Dimensional Fund Advisors was founded in 1981 after Booth's original Wells Fargo group was shut down, reuniting Booth with Myron Scholes, Merton Miller, Gene Fama, and his old boss Mac McQuown to build a new firm.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Shows DFA's founding bench strength (Nobel laureates and pioneering academics) as a structural source of its research-driven edge from day one.
insights.quote: we regrouped in '81 to start Dimensional

insights.claim: Dimensional launched in 1981 with only a small-cap fund and immediately entered the worst 9-year stretch of relative small-cap performance on record, with small stocks underperforming large stocks by the widest margin ever measured over a 9-year period.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A cautionary data point for anyone evaluating a factor strategy's early track record: a sound, well-researched thesis can post historically bad relative results for close to a decade before working.
insights.quote: Small stocks underperformed large stocks by the most they ever had over a 9-year period.

insights.claim: During Dimensional's first 9 years, its small-cap portfolio compounded at roughly 2% a year versus 14% annualized for the S&P 500 — yet the fund still slightly beat its own Russell 2000 benchmark, showing the manager delivered exactly what the asset class did.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Separates manager skill from asset-class performance: investors should judge a factor fund against its benchmark, not against the S&P 500, during periods when that factor is out of favor.
insights.quote: portfolio compounded at 2% a year, and the S&P 500 compounded at 14% a year

insights.claim: Despite the historically bad start, the small-cap premium reasserted itself over the following decades, with Booth stating the strategy worked out very well over the ensuing 35 years after that brutal first 9-year stretch.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Supports staying committed to a factor premium through multi-year underperformance rather than abandoning it after a bad decade, as the drought does not necessarily invalidate the long-run thesis.
insights.quote: it turns out over the last 35 years it has worked out very well, but that first 9 years was pretty nasty

insights.claim: A major institutional client confronted Booth near the trough of the small-cap drought, calling Dimensional the worst-performing manager in any asset category the client held; when Booth asked which part of the small-cap risk/return argument had actually changed, the client had no answer, stayed invested, and was later well rewarded.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A concrete case study in client retention through underperformance: separating whether the thesis changed from whether performance is currently disappointing is what kept a large account invested through the trough.
insights.quote: I just want you to know you're the worst performing manager we have in any asset category.

themes.theme: The Fama-French Three-Factor Model & Value Investing

insights.claim: The Fama-French three-factor model — adding size (large vs. small) and value (value vs. growth) factors to the market factor — replaced the single-factor CAPM/beta framework around 1991-92 and is, three decades later, still regarded as the last major theoretical breakthrough in investing.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A reminder that the multi-factor framework underlying most modern factor investing (size, value) has gone essentially unchallenged as the dominant academic model for over 30 years.
insights.quote: There's more than just the market. There's a size factor large versus small and then value versus growth.

insights.claim: Dimensional began seeding its value strategies based on a September 1991 pre-publication draft of the Fama-French paper that Booth personally carried to a client and to Fama's office, launching the funds before the research was formally published.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Illustrates a genuine information edge from proximity to primary academic research — DFA moved on the factor before the wider market had access to the published paper.
insights.quote: the value strategy started uh before the uh paper was published by Fama and French

themes.theme: Behavioral Investing: Staying Calm and the Sell Problem

insights.claim: Booth's rule of thumb for investor patience is that any sound strategy takes at least one year longer to pay off than an investor is willing to give it, meaning investors should mentally pre-commit to a longer holding period than feels comfortable.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A practical heuristic for setting holding-period expectations before entering a strategy, to avoid abandoning it right before it would have worked.
insights.quote: it all takes at least one year longer than you're willing to give it

insights.claim: Dimensional tells clients that the danger in fund selection is not the buy decision but the absence of a defined sell rule, since the natural temptation is to sell precisely when a fund underperforms — which could be this year, six years from now, or twenty years from now.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Investors should define an explicit sell discipline in advance and explicitly exclude relative underperformance as a trigger, since selling into a temporary drawdown is the most common way long-term premiums are missed.
insights.quote: The problem is the seduction will be you will sell this when it underperforms.

insights.claim: Booth's behavioral fix for panic-selling is to judge investment decisions by the quality of the decision at the time it was made rather than by the outcome, comparing it to a football play call that was correct even when the pass fails to connect.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A decision-quality framework investors and advisers can use to avoid overreacting to bad outcomes on sound decisions, reducing behaviorally-driven selling.
insights.quote: if you can convince people to judge themselves by the quality of the decision they made rather than the outcome, they'll be a lot better off

insights.claim: Ken French reportedly told the host it takes roughly 60-plus years of return history (he cited 64 years) to know with statistical confidence whether an actively managed fund's outperformance is skill rather than luck — far beyond any retail investor's realistic evaluation horizon.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Explains why short-term track records (1-5 years) are statistically close to meaningless for judging active manager skill, arguing against performance-chasing.
insights.quote: How long do we need to know statistically speaking if this active fund is any good and without blinking he said 64 years.

themes.theme: AI, the 'Gold Rush' Analogy, and Owning the Whole Market

insights.claim: Booth compares the AI investment theme to the California Gold Rush, where the biggest winner was Levi Strauss selling jeans to miners rather than a miner itself, arguing that AI being transformative does not tell an investor which specific companies will win or lose, so the rational response is to own the whole market rather than pick AI winners.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A structural argument against stock-picking within a hyped theme like AI: even correctly identifying that a technology will be huge gives little edge in identifying which specific stocks capture the value.
insights.quote: there's going to be big winners and big losers. And for our taste, that's why you want to buy all of them, I guess.

insights.claim: Booth says mega-cap technology stocks (the Magnificent Seven) have become such a large fraction of the overall market that client anxiety about concentration is now a dominant recurring conversation, echoing the FAANG-driven period roughly four to five years earlier that similarly squeezed out small-cap performance.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Flags mega-cap concentration risk as a live, top-of-mind client concern in 2026, comparable to a prior period that also weighed on small-cap relative returns.
insights.quote: They're such a big fraction the market now.

insights.claim: Using Fama-French's own historical return data going back 100 years, the host notes markets are about to enter the historically strongest 12-month window for small-cap value, with January 2027 standing out as the single best month of that seasonal 4-year cycle — while explicitly cautioning this is not a forecast he would trade on.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A seasonality pattern worth watching (not trading) in small-cap value heading into early 2027, framed by the host himself as historical curiosity rather than an actionable signal.
insights.quote: we're about to enter the 12 best months for small cap value. And the single best month of sort of this 12-month 4-year cycle is January 2027.

themes.theme: Compounding, Diversification & the Cost of Sitting in Cash

insights.claim: Dimensional crossed $1 trillion in assets under management in February 2026, a milestone Booth says produced the only other moment of visible excitement he has seen from Gene Fama besides the day Fama learned he'd won the Nobel Prize in Economics.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Marks a concrete AUM milestone (Feb 2026, $1T) for the firm and underscores the personal/academic pedigree still tied to its identity.
insights.quote: In February this year when we crossed a trillion dollars in assets under management.

insights.claim: Booth illustrates the cost of avoiding markets using his own family: $15,000 found in his late father's safe-deposit box (dating to 1945) would have grown to over $1 million if invested in the stock market by 1985, and would again be worth over $1 million if invested for the most recent 40-year stretch through today — evidence that his parents' generation's distrust of markets was directly costly.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A vivid, personal illustration of the opportunity cost of holding cash instead of equities across a 40-year horizon, useful for framing long-horizon compounding conversations with clients.

insights.claim: A dollar invested in the S&P 500 when Dimensional was founded in 1981 would be worth over $100 today (45 years later), versus roughly a fivefold increase in gold (from about $800/oz to roughly $4,200-4,400/oz) over the same period.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A direct 45-year comparison investors can use to contextualize gold's recent rally against equities' long-run compounding, despite gold bugs treating a 5x gain as vindication.
insights.quote: A dollar put in that S&P 500 when we started our fund, our firm, would be worth over $100 today after 45 years.

insights.claim: Dimensional keeps a wall of framed stock certificates from bankrupt companies in its Austin office as a reminder that individual stocks frequently go to zero while the aggregate stock market does not, which Booth cites as core empirical support for diversification over single-stock concentration.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A tangible framing device for explaining diversification's rationale to clients: single names carry real bankruptcy/zero risk that a market-cap-weighted market portfolio does not.
insights.quote: Individual stocks can go to zero. And the stock market is not going to zero. So, that's one of the arguments for diversification.

insights.claim: Dimensional cumulatively generated no earnings for its first 15 years, and Booth says the key to surviving was never doubting the underlying research-based idea — the only open question was whether the firm could survive long enough for performance to validate it.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: A reminder for founders and allocators evaluating early-stage investment firms that a sound research edge can take well over a decade to show up in both performance and profitability.
insights.quote: We never doubted we had a great idea. The question was always can we survive long enough

insights.claim: Dimensional's core distribution strategy for decades has been selling through education aimed at financial advisers — leading with research the firm believes matters rather than designing products calibrated to what would sell easily — on the premise that clients who understand the reasoning are less likely to redeem during drawdowns.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Explains DFA's historically low client attrition and advisor-channel-first go-to-market model as a deliberate structural choice tied to client retention through underperformance.
insights.quote: instead of designing products we think will sell, we go out with research and ideas we think are important and we try to convince people that they are important
